'''''Zostera marina''''' is a flowering [[vascular plant]] species as one of many kinds of [[seagrass]], with this species known primarily by the English name of '''common eelgrass''' or '''eelgrass''', with '''seawrack''' much less used, and refers to the plant after breaking loose from the submerged wetland soil, and drifting free with ocean current and waves to a coast seashore. It is a saline soft-sediment submerged plant native to [[Marine (ocean)|marine]] environments on the coastlines of northern latitudes from subtropical to subpolar regions of [[North America]] and [[Eurasia]].

==Distribution==
This species is the most wide-ranging marine [[flowering plant]] in the Northern Hemisphere and the most widespread species in the temperate northern hemisphere of Atlantic and Pacific Oceans.<ref>den Hartog, C. (1970). The seagrasses of the world. ''Verh K Ned Ak Wet Adf'' North-Holland, Amsterdam 59: 1–275. – in Möller, T. [http://www.helcom.fi/environment2/biodiv/endangered/Vascular_plants/en_GB/Zostera_marina/ ''Zostera marina'' (Linnaeus 1753), Eelgrass (Angiospermophyta).] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110717130057/http://www.helcom.fi/environment2/biodiv/endangered/Vascular_plants/en_GB/Zostera_marina/ |date=July 17, 2011 }} Helsinki Commission: Baltic Marine Environment Protection Commission.</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=Yan-Hao |last2=Zhao |first2=Xiang |last3=Tu |first3=Zhong |last4=Yan |first4=Wen-Jie |last5=Zhao |first5=Qi |last6=Zhang |first6=Pei-Dong |date=May 2024 |title=Propagating eelgrass ( Zostera marina ) from cuttings in land–sea combination systems: a novel method to improve the sustainability of seagrass restoration |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/rec.14103 |journal=Restoration Ecology |language=en |volume=32 |issue=4 |article-number=14103 |doi=10.1111/rec.14103 |bibcode=2024ResEc..3214103Z |issn=1061-2971|url-access=subscription }}</ref> It lives in cooler ocean waters in the [[North Atlantic]] and [[North Pacific]], and in the warmer southern parts of its range it dies off during warmer seasons.<ref name=fna>[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=200024703 Flora of North America]</ref> It grows in the [[Arctic]] region and endures several months of ice cover per year.<ref name=borum>Borum J., et al., (Eds.) (2004.) [http://www.seagrasses.org/handbook/european_seagrasses_low.pdf European seagrasses: an introduction to monitoring and management.] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110728010723/http://www.seagrasses.org/handbook/european_seagrasses_low.pdf |date=2011-07-28 }} European Union: Monitoring & Managing of European Seagrasses.</ref> It is the only seagrass known from [[Iceland]].<ref name=borum/> It can be found in [[bay]]s, [[lagoon]]s, [[estuary|estuaries]], on [[beach]]es, and in other coastal habitat. The several ecotypes each have specific habitat requirements.{{citation needed|date=March 2015}}  It occurs in calmer waters in the [[sublittoral]] zone, where it is rarely exposed to air.<ref name=fna/> It anchors via [[rhizome]]s in sandy or muddy substrates and its leaves catch particulate debris in the water which then collects around the bases of the plants, building up the top layer of the seabed.<ref name=fna/>

==Description and reproduction==
This flowering plant is a rhizomatous herb which produces a long stem with hairlike green leaves that measure up to {{ Convert | 1.2 | cm }} wide and may reach over {{ Convert | 1.0 | m }} long. It is a perennial plant, but it may grow as an annual.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Bos AR |author2=TJ Bouma |author3=GLJ de Kort |author4=Marieke M van Katwijk |name-list-style=amp |year=2007 |title=Ecosystem engineering by annual intertidal seagrass beds: Sediment accretion and modification |journal=[[Estuarine, Coastal and Shelf Science]] |volume=74 |issue= 1–2|pages=344–348 |doi=10.1016/j.ecss.2007.04.006 |bibcode=2007ECSS...74..344B |hdl=2066/34860 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> The rhizome grows horizontally through the substrate, anchoring via clusters of roots at nodes.<ref name=fna/> The plant is [[Plant sexuality|monoecious]], with an individual bearing both male and female flowers in separate alternating clusters. The inflorescence is about 10 cm long.<ref name="Parnell 12">Parnell, J. and Curtis, T. 2012. ''Webb's An Irish Flora.'' Cork University Press {{ISBN|978-185918-4783}}</ref> The fruit is a nutlet with a transparent coat containing the seed. The plant can also undergo [[vegetative reproduction]], sprouting repeatedly from its rhizome and spreading into a meadow-like colony on the seabed known as a [[Clonal colony|genet]].<ref name=fonseca>Fonseca, M., et al. (2003). [http://mapping2.orr.noaa.gov/portal/subtidal/meta/fonseca_eelgrass_report.pdf NOAA joint pilot project on eelgrass (''Zostera marina'' L.) recovery in San Francisco Bay.] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721060227/http://mapping2.orr.noaa.gov/portal/subtidal/meta/fonseca_eelgrass_report.pdf |date=July 21, 2011 }} NOAA National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science.</ref> One meadow of cloned eelgrass was determined to be 3000 years old, genetically.<ref name=borum/> When undergoing [[sexual reproduction]], the plant produces large quantities of seeds, at times numbering several thousand seeds per square meter of plants.<ref name=borum/> The plant [[biological dispersal|disperses]] large distances when its stems break away and carry the fertile seeds to new areas, eventually dropping to the seabed.<ref name=borum/> The seagrass is a favorite food of several species of [[waterfowl]], which may also distribute the seeds.<ref name=borum/>

==Ecology==
This ''Zostera'' grows in muddy and sandy shores only at and below spring tides.<ref name="Parnell 12"/> This plant is an important member of the coastal ecosystem in many areas because it helps to physically form the habitat and it plays a crucial role for many other species.<ref name=borum/><ref name=wyllie>Wyllie-Echeverria, S. and M. Fonseca. (2003). [http://mapping2.orr.noaa.gov/portal/subtidal/pdfs/projectreports/partnership_seagrassrev_fin.pdf Eelgrass (''Zostera marina'' L.) in San Francisco Bay, California from 1920 to the present.] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721060246/http://mapping2.orr.noaa.gov/portal/subtidal/pdfs/projectreports/partnership_seagrassrev_fin.pdf |date=July 21, 2011 }} NOAA National Centers for Coastal Ocean Science.</ref> For example, it provides a sheltered [[spawning]] ground for the [[Pacific herring]] (''Clupea pallasii'').<ref name=wyllie/> Juvenile [[Atlantic cod]] (''Gadus morhua'') hide in eelgrass beds as they grow.<ref name=hanson>Hanson, A. R. (2004). [http://www.bofep.org/PDFfiles/Eelgrass_Technica_%20Report.pdf Status and conservation of eelgrass (''Zostera marina'') in eastern Canada.] Canadian Wildlife Service Technical Report Series #412.</ref> The [[blue mussel]] (''Mytilus edulis'') attaches to its leaves.<ref name=borum/> The [[green algae|green alga]] ''[[Entocladia perforans]]'', an [[endophyte]], depends on this eelgrass.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.ukmarinesac.org.uk/communities/habitats-review/hr22_3.htm |title=UK Marine Special Areas of Conservation |access-date=2010-12-11 |archive-date=2011-07-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110721031625/http://www.ukmarinesac.org.uk/communities/habitats-review/hr22_3.htm }}</ref> A great many animals use the plant for food, including the [[isopoda|isopod]] ''[[Idotea chelipes]]'' and the purple sea urchin ''[[Paracentrotus lividus]]''.<ref name=borum/> The [[brant goose|Atlantic brant]] (''Branta bernicula hrota'') subsists almost entirely on the plant.<ref name=hanson/> When the eelgrass dies, detaches, and washes up on the beach, a whole new [[ecosystem]] is founded; many species of insects and other invertebrates begin to inhabit the dead plant, including the [[amphipod]] ''[[Talitrus saltator]]'', the [[diptera|fly]] ''[[Fucellia tergina]]'', and the [[beetle]]s ''[[Stenus biguttatus]]'',  ''[[Paederus littoralis]]'', and ''[[Coccinella septempunctata]]''.<ref>Jedrzejczak, M. F. (2002). [http://www.vliz.be/imisdocs/publications/99188.pdf Stranded ''Zostera marina'' L. vs wrack fauna community interactions on a Baltic sandy beach (Hel, Poland): A short term pilot study, Part II.] ''Oceanologia'' 44:3 367–87.</ref>

The [[bacteria]]l species ''[[Granulosicoccus coccoides]]'' was first isolated from the leaves of the plant.<ref name=kuri>Kurilenko, V. V., et al. (2010). ''Granulosicoccus coccoides'' sp. nov., isolated from leaves of seagrass (''Zostera marina''). ''Int J Syst Evol Microbiol'' 60 972–76.</ref>

==Threats==
Populations of the plant have been damaged by a number of processes, especially increased [[turbidity]] in the water; like most other plants, eelgrass requires sunlight to grow.<ref name=wyllie/> One plant may adapt to light level by growing longer leaves to reach the sun in low-light areas; individuals in clear or shallow water may have leaves a few centimeters long, while individuals in deeper spots may have leaves over a meter long.<ref name=borum/> Human activities such as [[dredging]] and [[trawling]] damage eelgrass meadows; practices used in [[scallop]] and [[mussel]] harvesting in the [[Wadden Sea]] have cleared much eelgrass from the sea bottom there.<ref name=borum/> [[Aquaculture]] operations and coastal development destroy colonies.<ref name=borum/> [[Water pollution|Pollution]] from many sources, including riverside [[farm]]s, [[sewage]] lines,<ref name="Jones et al., 2018">{{cite journal | doi=10.3389/fpls.2018.00133| pmid=29467789 | title=Tracking Nitrogen Source Using δ15N Reveals Human and Agricultural Drivers of Seagrass Degradation across the British Isles | journal=Frontiers in Plant Science| volume=9 | article-number=133 | last1 = Jones | first1 = BJ | last2 = Cullen-Unsworth | first2 = LC | last3 = Unsworth | first3 = RKF| year=2018 | pmc = 5808166 | doi-access=free }}</ref> fish processing plants, and [[oil spill]]s, damage eelgrass meadows.<ref name=hanson/> Conservation and restoration efforts of ''Zostera marina'' habitats<ref>{{cite journal |author1=Bos, Arthur R |author2=Marieke M. van Katwijk |name-list-style=amp |year=2007 |title=Planting density, hydrodynamic exposure and mussel beds affect survival of transplanted intertidal eelgrass |journal=Marine Ecology Progress Series |volume=336 |pages=121–129 |doi=10.3354/meps336121 |bibcode=2007MEPS..336..121B |url=http://science.naturalis.nl/media/341375/bos%202007%20meps336%20-%20affecting%20eelgrass%20survival.pdf |doi-access=free }}{{Dead link|date=October 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |author=van Katwijk MM |author2=AR Bos |author3=VN de Jonge |author4=LSAM Hanssen |author5=DCR Hermus |author6=DJ de Jong |name-list-style=amp |year=2009 |title=Guidelines for seagrass restoration: Importance of habitat selection and donor population, spreading of risks, and ecosystem engineering effects |journal=Marine Pollution Bulletin |volume=58 |issue= 2|pages=179–188 |doi= 10.1016/j.marpolbul.2008.09.028|pmid= 19131078|bibcode=2009MarPB..58..179V |hdl=2066/75284 |hdl-access=free }}</ref> including transplants and seed-based <ref>{{Cite journal |last=Infantes |first=E |last2=Eriander |first2=L |last3=Moksnes |first3=P-O |date=2016 |title=Eelgrass (Zostera marina) restoration on the west coast of Sweden using seeds |url=http://www.int-res.com/abstracts/meps/v546/p31-45/ |journal=Marine Ecology Progress Series |language=en |volume=546 |pages=31-45 |doi=10.3354/meps11615 |issn=0171-8630}}</ref> restoration, have increased since their rapid decline started several decades ago.

[[Invasive species]] have been shown to have a negative effect on eelgrass and associated ecosystems. In [[Nova Scotia]], the invasive  [[European green crab]] (''Carcinus maenas'') destroys eelgrass when it digs in the substrate for prey items.<ref name=hanson/>  Experimental work in Sweden has also shown that seed predation by the shore crab ''Carcinus maenas'' can reduce eelgrass recruitment, potentially contributing to feedbacks that slow natural recovery of degraded meadows.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Infantes|first1=Eduardo|last2=Crouzy|first2=Caroline|last3=Per-Olav|first3=Moksnes|title=Seed Predation by the Shore Crab Carcinus maenas: A Positive Feedback Preventing Eelgrass Recovery?|journal=PLOS ONE|date=2016|volume=11|issue=12|article-number=e0168128|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0168128|pmid=27977802|pmc=5157998|bibcode=2016PLoSO..1168128I|doi-access=free}}</ref> The decline of eelgrass in [[Antigonish, Nova Scotia|Antigonish Harbour]] has resulted in fewer [[Canada goose|Canada geese]], which feed on the rhizome, and fewer [[common goldeneye]], which eat [[invertebrate]]s that live in eelgrass meadows.<ref name=hanson/>

The [[slime mold]] ''[[Labyrinthula zosterae]]'' caused a "wasting disease" of eelgrass resulting in large-scale losses in the 1930s; localized populations are still affected by the slime mold today.<ref name=borum/> During this time, populations of the eelgrass-eating Atlantic brant dropped.<ref name=hanson/> Remaining geese ate less-preferred food plants and algae, and hunters subsequently noticed that brant meat began to taste different.<ref name=hanson/> Even today, brants no longer [[bird migration|migrate]] over the Nova Scotia area.<ref name=hanson/>

== Genomics and evolutionary adaptations ==
The ''Zostera marina'' [[genome]] has been [[Sequencing|sequenced]] and analyzed by Olsen ''et al.'' in 2016 and the resulting article has been published in [[Nature (journal)|Nature]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Olsen|first1=Jeanine L.|last2=Rouzé|first2=Pierre|last3=Verhelst|first3=Bram|last4=Lin|first4=Yao-Cheng|last5=Bayer|first5=Till|last6=Collen|first6=Jonas|last7=Dattolo|first7=Emanuela|last8=De Paoli|first8=Emanuele|last9=Dittami|first9=Simon|date=2016-02-18|title=The genome of the seagrass Zostera marina reveals angiosperm adaptation to the sea|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=530|issue=7590|pages=331–335|doi=10.1038/nature16548|pmid=26814964|bibcode=2016Natur.530..331O|issn=0028-0836|hdl=11250/2386505|doi-access=free|hdl-access=free}}</ref> The approximate genome sequence of ''Z. marina'' is 202.3 Mb and encodes approximately 20450 [[protein]]-coding genes (of which 86,6% are supported by [[transcriptome]] data). The assembled genome was found to consist of large numbers of [[repeat element]]s accounting for 63% of the assembled genome. The researchers revealed key adaptations at the molecular biological level that have occurred during evolution of ''Z. marina'', an [[Flowering plant|angiosperm]] that has adopted a marine lifestyle. Genome analysis revealed that ''Z. marina'' lost the entire repertoire of [[stoma]]tal genes, genes involved in volatile compound biosynthesis and signaling (such as [[ethylene]] and [[terpenoid]]s) as well as genes for [[ultraviolet]] protection and [[phytochrome]]s used for far-red sensing. Besides these gene losses, also gene gain events have been described, mostly involving the adjustment to full salinity and ion [[homeostasis]]. Also macro-algae like cell wall components (low-methylated polyanionic [[pectin]]s and sulfated galactans) have been described, unique for ''Z. marina'' compared to other angiosperms.

==Human uses==
[[File:Tangtag paa Laesoe 2011 ubt-032.JPG|thumb|right|An example of traditional [[seaweed roofs on Læsø]], Denmark]]
People have long used this plant species as [[Thatching|roof thatching]] in some areas.<ref name=borum/> On [[Læsø]] in Denmark, a [[Seaweed roofs on Læsø|tradition of using eelgrass as roof material]] is recognised by being included on the [[Tentative List of World Heritage Sites]] since 2023.<ref name=tentativelist>{{cite web |author=<!-- not stated --> |date= 2023|title= Seaweed Houses and Sea-salt Huts, Laesoe Island|url= https://whc.unesco.org/en/tentativelists/6692/|website= |location= |publisher= [[UNESCO]]|access-date=30 April 2026}}</ref> It has been used as [[fertilizer]] and [[cattle]] [[fodder]] in [[Norway]] for centuries.<ref name=alm>Alm, T. (2003). "On the uses of ''Zostera marina'', mainly in Norway." ''Economic Botany'' 57:4 640–45.  {{JSTOR|4256745}}</ref> It has also been dried and used as stuffing for [[mattress]]es and furniture.<ref name=alm/> The [[Seri people|Seri]] hunter gatherers of Mexico eat eelgrass grains after toasting them and grinding into a paste.

[[Ángel León (chef)|Ángel León]], a Spanish chef, has planted meadows of ''Z. marina'' (described as "sea rice") in the [[Bay of Cádiz]] in order to harvest the grains. The texture is described as between rice and [[quinoa]], but with a more saline flavour. It is gluten-free and high in fibre.<ref>{{Cite magazine|title=Seeding the Ocean: Inside a Michelin-Starred Chef's Revolutionary Quest to Harvest Rice From the Sea|url=https://time.com/5926780/chef-angel-leon-sea-rice/|access-date=13 October 2023|magazine=Time|last=Goulding|first=Matt|others=Photographs by Paolo Verzone|date=9 January 2021|archive-date=26 September 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230926234449/https://time.com/5926780/chef-angel-leon-sea-rice/|url-status=dead}}</ref>
